query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended as energetic structural materials, what single testable hypothesis identifies an intervention that could improve ductility and uniform deformability without sacrificing high strength or impact-induced energy release? State the proposed intervention, its hypothesized mechanism, the improvement expected relative to the untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Microalloying an Al- and early-transition-metal-rich refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) with trace boron (≈0.05–0.15 at%) followed by a homogenize-plus-quench treatment that promotes boron grain-boundary segregation (without bulk boride precipitation) will increase room-temperature uniform elongation and delay strain localization (more uniform deformability) while maintaining high yield/ultimate strength and not measurably reducing impact-induced specific energy release.
generation.material_initial_state: Polycrystalline Al-containing refractory HEA with a predominantly BCC matrix (e.g., a Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr–Al family composition) processed to a single-phase or BCC-dominant microstructure, oxygen content typical of vacuum arc melting (~hundreds of ppm), grain size 10–50 µm, no intentional interstitial additions, baseline exhibiting limited room-temperature ductility and strong work hardening but early localization.
generation.intervention: Add 0.1 at% B (target range 0.05–0.15 at%) to the melt, then homogenize at 1100–1200 °C for 4–12 h in high vacuum or inert atmosphere and water quench to trap B at grain boundaries; avoid slow cooling through 900–700 °C that would form borides.
generation.conditions: Room temperature (20–30 °C), quasi-static tensile strain rate 1e-3–1e-2 s^-1 in air; impact tests in air at ambient pressure; alloy chemistry retains a majority of oxidizable elements (Al + Ti + Zr + Hf ≥ 40 at%) to preserve energetic reactivity; total interstitial O ≤ 1000 ppm after processing.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanometer-scale boron segregation layers at prior-austenite-equivalent grain boundaries in the BCC matrix (verified by APT or STEM-EDS/EELS), with no continuous boride films and ≤1 vol% discrete boride particles; boundaries remain clean and cohesive; dislocation slip spans multiple grains with enhanced storage (higher work hardening rate).
generation.mechanism: Boron segregates to grain boundaries, increases boundary cohesive energy, and competitively displaces embrittling oxygen from boundaries. This suppresses intergranular crack initiation and delays strain localization, enabling more uniform plastic flow and higher uniform elongation. Because B content is trace and resides mainly at boundaries, bulk lattice friction and solid-solution strengthening remain high, preserving yield and ultimate strength. The energetic response is maintained because the major oxidizable constituents (Al, Ti, Zr, Hf) and their oxidation thermochemistry are unchanged; trace B does not significantly diminish the alloy’s impact-induced oxidation/combustion energy release.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline alloy (same composition minus B, same thermal history), the B-microalloyed and quenched condition will show: (i) an increase in room-temperature uniform elongation by roughly +3 to +8 absolute percentage points (e.g., from 1–3% to 4–10%), (ii) yield strength and UTS within ±10% of baseline (UTS potentially slightly higher if work hardening is improved), and (iii) impact-induced specific energy release (J/g) within ±10% of baseline (no statistically significant decrease). Fractography will transition from predominantly intergranular or mixed modes to more transgranular dimpled features.
generation.baseline: The same Al- and early-transition-metal-rich RHEA without boron, melted and processed identically (homogenize at 1100–1200 °C and quench), tested under the same mechanical and impact conditions.
generation.boundary: If boron exceeds ~0.2 at% or cooling is slow enough to form continuous boride films or >1 vol% coarse borides, ductility may degrade. Very high oxygen (>1000–1500 ppm) can tie up B as BOx or borates, preventing GB segregation and nullifying benefits. At elevated temperatures (>700 °C), grain-boundary cohesion may be less rate-limiting, reducing the observed ductility gain. Compositions with low oxidizable content (Al + Ti + Zr + Hf < 30 at%) may not qualify as energetic structural materials, making the energy-release criterion irrelevant.
generation.uncertainty: No direct prior evidence is provided here; the expected magnitude of ductility improvement and strength retention is uncertain and could vary with exact composition, oxygen level, and thermal history. There is also uncertainty about avoiding boride precipitation across different RHEA chemistries during cooling.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two heats of the same Al- and early-transition-metal-rich RHEA: (A) baseline (no B) and (B) +0.1 at% B. Melt and cast identically under vacuum; homogenize both at 1150 °C for 8 h in high-purity Ar or vacuum and water-quench. Verify oxygen content. Characterize microstructure (XRD, SEM-EBSD for grain size, TEM for second phases). Use APT or STEM-EDS/EELS line scans across grain boundaries to confirm B segregation in (B) and its absence in (A); quantify boride volume fraction (<1 vol% criterion). Perform room-temperature uniaxial tensile tests (n ≥ 5 per condition) at 1e-3 s^-1 to obtain 0.2% yield strength, UTS, uniform elongation, and work-hardening rate. Conduct instrumented drop-weight impact tests on thin coupons in air with high-speed IR thermography and post-mortem mass gain to estimate specific energy release (J/g) using oxidation enthalpies; compare to baseline. Fractography by SEM to assess failure mode.
measurements: Boron distribution at grain boundaries (APT or STEM-EDS/EELS concentration profiles, monolayer enrichment factor)
Tensile 0.2% yield strength, UTS, uniform elongation, n-value
Specific energy release during impact (J/g) from IR calorimetry and oxidation mass gain
Fracture surface mode fraction (intergranular vs transgranular)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if any of the following are observed: (1) the B-added condition does not increase uniform elongation by at least +3 absolute percentage points over baseline or shows a decrease; (2) yield strength or UTS decrease by more than 10% relative to baseline; (3) specific energy release decreases by more than 10% relative to baseline; or (4) APT/STEM shows no measurable B grain-boundary enrichment while boride volume fraction exceeds 1 vol%.
